p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Every year thousands of patients die while waiting for a kidney, liver or heart, although the organs that could have saved them were buried or cremated with donors who had never been asked. The shortage is not, at root, medical. Transplant surgery is well established, and a single deceased donor can save or transform several lives. The obstacles lie in hesitation, misunderstanding and the circumstances in which the question must be asked. Brain death is an unfamiliar concept to many families, who see a loved one's chest still rising on a ventilator and cannot accept that death has occurred. The request for donation comes at a moment of acute grief, often from hospital staff who have had no training in how to make it.

Some countries have responded by presuming consent unless a person has registered an objection. Such laws can raise donation rates, but they are no substitute for public trust; where families feel pressured or suspicious, they may refuse regardless of what the law presumes. The deeper safeguard is transparency. When the allocation of organs follows clear and public rules, when the declaration of death is kept entirely separate from the transplant team, and when grieving families are treated with patience rather than urgency, more of them say yes. A system that is trusted will rarely lack donors; a system that is suspected will always lack them.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: A museum is often imagined as a neutral storehouse, a place where objects from the past are simply kept safe and placed on display. Yet every museum is the result of choices. Someone decided which objects were worth collecting and which were left to decay; someone wrote the labels that tell visitors what an object means. A bronze image displayed under glass as an example of a dynastic style may once have been carried in procession by worshippers to whom it was not art at all, but a living presence. A farming implement may be shown as a curiosity, with no mention of the hands that shaped it or the skill required to use it. Such choices are rarely malicious, but they quietly shape what a society remembers and what it forgets.

In recent years, many museums have begun to share this authority. They invite communities to help interpret collections drawn from their own traditions, record the oral histories that accompany objects, and acknowledge openly when an item was acquired in circumstances that would not be accepted today. Critics complain that this turns the museum into a forum for argument rather than a place of quiet contemplation. But argument may be a sign of health. A museum that presents a single, settled story invites admiration; one that admits the past is contested invites understanding.

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
opts: The organ shortage stems from mistrust and misunderstanding, and is best addressed by transparent, humane systems.
Families should be pressed for a quick decision on donation.
The organ shortage exists because transplant surgery is still experimental.
Presumed-consent laws alone can solve the organ shortage.
questions.why: Main idea: 'The shortage is not, at root, medical', and 'The deeper safeguard is transparency'.

questions.q: According to the passage, why do many families find it hard to accept brain death?
opts: They see the patient's chest still rising on a ventilator.
The law does not recognise brain death.
Doctors refuse to explain the diagnosis.
The patient is usually conscious.
questions.why: Detail: families 'see a loved one's chest still rising on a ventilator and cannot accept that death has occurred'.

questions.q: Keeping the declaration of death separate from the transplant team is most likely intended to:
opts: prevent families from registering objections.
reassure families that death is not declared hastily in order to obtain organs.
allow transplant surgeons to work more quickly.
reduce the cost of transplant surgery.
questions.why: Inference: the measure is listed under transparency that builds trust; families who are 'suspicious' may refuse.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards presumed-consent laws is:
opts: wholly opposed to them as immoral.
unreservedly enthusiastic.
cautious, granting that they may help but insisting they cannot replace trust.
indifferent to their effects.
questions.why: Tone: 'Such laws can raise donation rates, but they are no substitute for public trust'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'acute' means:
opts: intense and severe
clever and perceptive
long-lasting but mild
sharply pointed
questions.why: Vocabulary: 'a moment of acute grief' is a moment of overwhelming sorrow.

questions.q: The passage mainly argues that museums:
opts: are neutral storehouses that simply preserve objects.
shape collective memory through their choices and gain by sharing interpretive authority.
should display only objects of artistic value.
ought to avoid any form of public debate.
questions.why: Main idea: 'every museum is the result of choices' that 'shape what a society remembers', and sharing authority leads to 'understanding'.

questions.q: According to the passage, what have many museums begun to do in recent years?
opts: Invite communities to help interpret collections and record oral histories.
Display only farming implements.
Remove labels from their exhibits.
Return all their objects to the original owners.
questions.why: Detail: 'They invite communities to help interpret collections... record the oral histories that accompany objects'.

questions.q: The example of the bronze image suggests that:
opts: museums should not display religious objects at all.
worshippers regarded the image mainly as an example of style.
displaying an object as art may strip it of the meaning it held for those who used it.
bronze images were never used in religious processions.
questions.why: Inference: to its worshippers it 'was not art at all, but a living presence', a meaning the museum label may omit.

questions.q: How does the author respond to the critics mentioned in the passage?
opts: With angry dismissal of their concerns.
With respectful disagreement, suggesting that debate may be healthy.
By ignoring their objection altogether.
With complete agreement that museums should avoid argument.
questions.why: Tone: 'But argument may be a sign of health.'

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'contested' means:
opts: won in a competition
subject to dispute and differing interpretations
officially approved
forgotten by later generations
questions.why: Vocabulary: a past that is 'contested' is contrasted with 'a single, settled story'.
